'''Herbert John Ryser''' (July 28, 1923 &ndash; July 12, 1985) was a professor of mathematics, widely regarded as one of the major figures in [[combinatorics]] in the 20th century.<ref name=ohio>[http://www.math.ohio-state.edu/history/biographies/hjryser/ Ryser's biography] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081031035552/http://www.math.ohio-state.edu/history/biographies/hjryser/ |date=2008-10-31 }} at the [[Ohio State University]] website</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Matrices in combinatorics and graph theory By, x|year=2000|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-0-7923-6469-6|pages=xi|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=L5EyBHUYpRYC&pg=PR11 |author=Bolian Liu|author2=Hong-Jian Lai |accessdate=7 January 2011|quote=...Herbert John Ryser, who can rightfully be considered the father of Combinatorial Matrix Theory...}}</ref> He is the namesake of the [[Bruck–Ryser–Chowla theorem]], [[Ryser's formula]] for the [[computation of the permanent of a matrix]], and [[Ryser's conjecture]].

==Early life==
Ryser was born to the family of Fred G. and Edna (Huels) Ryser. He received the B.A. (1945), M.A. (1947), and Ph.D. (1948) from the [[University of Wisconsin]].<ref name=brualdi>Richard A. Brualdi: "In memoriam: Herbert J. Ryser", ''Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A'' 47(1) (January 1988), pp. 1–5</ref> His doctoral thesis "Rational Vector Spaces" was supervised by [[Cornelius Joseph Everett, Jr.]] and [[Cyrus Colton MacDuffee|Cyrus C. MacDuffee]].<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=10321}}</ref>  (Ryser was Everett's only doctoral student.)<ref name="Lagarias2010">{{cite book|last=Lagarias|first=Jeffrey C.|title=The ultimate challenge: the 3x+1 problem|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hekJ7JDMEVkC&pg=PA228|accessdate=27 June 2011|year=2010|publisher=American Mathematical Soc.|isbn=978-0-8218-4940-8|pages=228–}}</ref>

==Career==
After his Ph.D., Ryser spent a year at Princeton's [[Institute for Advanced Study]], then joined the faculty of [[Ohio State University]]. In 1962 he took a professorship at [[Syracuse University]], and in 1967 moved to [[Caltech]].<ref>{{cite news
|newspaper=Engineering & Science Magazine
|page=30	
|title=Emeritus Professors – 1985
|date=September 1985
|url=http://calteches.library.caltech.edu/595/02/Emeritus.pdf
|accessdate=2010-07-18
}}</ref> His doctoral students include [[Richard A. Brualdi]], [[Clement W. H. Lam]], and [[Marion Tinsley]].

Ryser contributed to the theory of [[combinatorial design]]s, finite [[set system]]s, the [[Permanent (mathematics)|permanent]], combinatorial functions, and to many other topics in combinatorics.<ref name=ohio/> He served as editor of the journals ''[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]]'', ''[[Linear and Multilinear Algebra]]'', and ''[[Journal of Algebra]]''.<ref name=ohio/> Ryser's estate funded an endowment creating undergraduate mathematics scholarships at Caltech known as the H. J. Ryser Scholarships.<ref name="ctech">California Tech, "Mathematics Awards", May 17, 1991, page 1.  (Scan of that page on-line [http://caltechcampuspubs.library.caltech.edu/1487/1/1991_05_17_92_27.pdf via on-line archives at the newspaper].)</ref>

The ''Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A'' denoted two issues after Ryser's passing as the "Herbert J. Ryser Memorial Issue", parts 1 and 2.<ref>{{cite journal|journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A]]|year=1988|volume=47|issue=2|title=Papers to Appear in The Herbert J. Ryser Memorial Issue, Part Ii|author=Richard A. Brualdi|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0ITxAAAAMAAJ&q=%22herbert+j+ryser+memorial+issue%22+%22part+ii%22|accessdate=7 January 2011}}</ref>
